country.name: Italy
country.summary: Italy grows wine in every one of its twenty regions and trades places with France as the largest producer on earth. Its vines are mostly native: Sangiovese, Nebbiolo, Barbera, Montepulciano, Corvina, Aglianico, Nero d'Avola and Primitivo for red; Glera, Garganega, Trebbiano, Cortese, Verdicchio, Fiano and Vermentino for white; hundreds more behind them. The law is an EU pyramid with Italian names, DOCG and DOC above IGT with plain vino at the base, and the words Classico, Riserva and Superiore attach to the appellation rather than to a vineyard rank. The exam leans hardest on Piedmont, Tuscany and Veneto: the ageing rules of Barolo, Barbaresco, Brunello and Chianti Classico, the place-versus-grape traps, and the three ways Veneto treats one blend.
country.overview:
The Greeks called the south Oenotria, the land of trained vines, and the Romans carried the vine north to the Alps; the shape of Italian wine has not changed much since. Vines grow everywhere because the peninsula is a spine of hills, the Apennines, between two seas, with the Alps across the top and two large islands below. Altitude and the sea are the two levers: the north is continental and alpine, the centre is hill country, the south and the islands are Mediterranean and plant high to escape the heat.

The law came late. The first DOC rules date from 1963, the first DOCs were granted in 1966 (Vernaccia di San Gimignano was the first), and the first DOCGs in 1980 went to Brunello di Montalcino, Barolo, Barbaresco and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano. In 1992 the Goria law added IGT, the broad geographic tier that gave a legal home to the Super Tuscans, which had been selling as table wine for twenty years. The EU reform that took effect in 2009 folded DOCG and DOC into DOP and IGT into IGP, and Italy kept its own words on the label. Under the current code an IGT must stand for five years before it can become a DOC, and a DOC for seven before DOCG.

Read a DOCG as a promise of control, not of quality: a numbered state strip across the capsule (the fascetta), tasting by panel, tighter yields and longer ageing. Some of the country's most expensive wines are IGT by choice. Learn each appellation's own meaning for Riserva and Superiore, because the minimums differ from one to the next, and read Classico as the historic heart of a zone rather than a rank.

The exam divides Italy north and south. North means Nebbiolo in Piedmont, the traditional method in Franciacorta and Trento, tank Prosecco, Soave and the Valpolicella family in Veneto, and alpine whites in Alto Adige and Friuli. Centre and south means Sangiovese in Tuscany and its three great DOCGs, the Montepulciano name trap, Aglianico in Campania and Basilicata, Primitivo and Negroamaro in Puglia, Etna and Marsala in Sicily, Cannonau and Vermentino in Sardinia. Hold the grape behind every place name and the method behind every style, and the rest is geography.

grapes.name: Sangiovese
grapes.styles: Italy's most planted grape: Chianti, Brunello, Vino Nobile, Morellino, Romagna. High acid, firm tannin, sour cherry, mid colour.

grapes.name: Nebbiolo
grapes.styles: Barolo, Barbaresco, Roero, Gattinara, Valtellina: pale, tannic, acid, tar and rose.

grapes.name: Montepulciano
grapes.styles: The grape of Abruzzo and the Marche (Rosso Conero): dark, soft, generous. Not the Tuscan town of Vino Nobile, whose grape is Sangiovese.

grapes.name: Barbera
grapes.styles: Piedmont's everyday red, high acid, low tannin: Asti, Alba, Nizza.

grapes.name: Corvina
grapes.styles: Valpolicella, Amarone, Recioto and Bardolino.

grapes.name: Aglianico
grapes.styles: Taurasi in Campania and Aglianico del Vulture in Basilicata: late, tannic, age-worthy.

grapes.name: Nero d'Avola
grapes.styles: Sicily's red, dark and warm; lightened by Frappato in Cerasuolo di Vittoria.

grapes.name: Zinfandel
grapes.styles: Called Primitivo in Puglia, where it makes ripe, sweet-fruited reds in Manduria and Gioia del Colle; DNA proved it the same vine as California's Zinfandel.

grapes.name: Glera
grapes.styles: Prosecco, by the tank method.

grapes.name: Garganega
grapes.styles: Soave and Gambellara, dry and as Recioto.

grapes.name: Trebbiano Toscano
grapes.styles: The neutral, high-yielding white of central Italy, Ugni Blanc in France; Trebbiano d'Abruzzo is a different grape.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: The commercial white of the north-east: Delle Venezie DOC, Alto Adige, Friuli.

grapes.name: Vermentino
grapes.styles: Sardinia (Gallura DOCG), Liguria and the Tuscan coast: fresh, herbal, saline.

grapes.name: Verdicchio
grapes.styles: The Marche's age-worthy white, Castelli di Jesi and Matelica; the same vine as Trebbiano di Soave and Lugana's Turbiana.

grapes.name: Fiano
grapes.styles: Campania's waxy, nutty white of Avellino.

grapes.name: Greco
grapes.styles: Greco di Tufo, stony and firm, from the same Irpinian hills.

grapes.name: Nerello Mascalese
grapes.styles: Etna's pale, taut, high-altitude red.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc
grapes.styles: Moscato Bianco in Asti and Moscato d'Asti; Zibibbo, which is Muscat of Alexandria, on Pantelleria.

grapes.name: Sagrantino
grapes.styles: Montefalco's ferociously tannic red, dry and passito.

grapes.name: Cortese
grapes.styles: Gavi, the lean white of south-east Piedmont.

grapes.name: Dolcetto
grapes.styles: Piedmont's early, soft, dry red.

grapes.name: Lambrusco
grapes.styles: A family of Emilian grapes making frizzante red in tank.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Franciacorta, Trento, Alto Adige and Sicily; a growing still-wine presence.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The most planted international red, from Friuli's plain to Bolgheri.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Bolgheri and the Super Tuscans; Carmignano's old exception inside a DOCG.

exam: The pyramid, DOCG to vino, with its dates: 1963 law, 1966 first DOCs, 1980 first DOCGs, 1992 IGT, 2009 DOP and IGP.
What DOCG adds: the fascetta, panel tasting, stricter yields and ageing; why it is not a quality guarantee.
Classico, Riserva, Superiore: what each means, and that Riserva's months are set per appellation.
The grape behind every place name: Barolo, Gavi, Soave, Taurasi, Vino Nobile, Montalcino, Vittoria, Gallura.
Methods behind styles: appassimento (Amarone, Recioto, Sforzato), tank (Prosecco, Asti, Lambrusco), bottle (Franciacorta, Trento, Alta Langa), fortified (Marsala).
The Super Tuscans and IGT; Sassicaia's own DOC.
The Montepulciano trap and the Vulture-versus-Taurasi trap.
traps: DOCG is a control level, not a quality rank; a Toscana IGT can outprice every DOCG on the list.
Montepulciano is a Tuscan town (Vino Nobile, Sangiovese) and an Abruzzese grape (Montepulciano d'Abruzzo); never the same wine.
Riserva has no national minimum; each disciplinare sets it, from a year to five.
Classico is the old heart of a zone, not a higher tier; Chianti Classico is a separate DOCG from Chianti.
Prosecco, Asti and Lambrusco are tank method; Franciacorta, Trento and Alta Langa are bottle fermented.
Amarone is dry, Recioto sweet, Ripasso neither; Sforzato is Valtellina's dried-grape dry Nebbiolo.
Trebbiano d'Abruzzo and Trebbiano di Soave are not Trebbiano Toscano; Bonarda means three different grapes in three places.
Vino da Tavola is gone; the base tier is simply Vino, and a Vino Varietale may name its grape.

Classico: the historic core of a zone. Riserva: longer ageing, months set per appellation. Superiore: higher minimum alcohol, often lower yields or more age.

cards.f: Sweetness words on an Italian label
cards.b: Secco dry; Abboccato off-dry; Amabile medium sweet; Dolce sweet. Frizzante lightly sparkling, Spumante fully sparkling; Passito from dried grapes.

cards.f: Promotion rules under the current code
cards.b: An IGT must exist five years before it can become a DOC; a DOC seven years before DOCG.
Vino Nobile di Montepulciano: Sangiovese (Prugnolo Gentile) from the Tuscan hill town. Montepulciano d'Abruzzo: the Montepulciano grape grown in Abruzzo.
Tank (Martinotti or Charmat): Prosecco, Asti, Lambrusco. Bottle (Metodo Classico): Franciacorta, Trento, Alta Langa, Oltrepò Pavese. Bottle refermented, undisgorged: col fondo Prosecco.

questions.q: In which year did Italy grant its first DOCGs?
questions.exp: The first DOCGs, Brunello di Montalcino, Barolo, Barbaresco and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, came in 1980. The DOC law dates from 1963, the first DOCs from 1966, IGT from 1992.

questions.q: Which tier did the 1992 Goria law create?
questions.exp: The Goria law of 1992 added IGT, the broad geographic tier, and gave the Super Tuscans a home above table wine. DOC came in 1963 and DOCG was first awarded in 1980.

questions.q: What does the word Classico mark on an Italian label?
opts: The historic heart of the zone
questions.exp: Classico is the original core of a denomination, as in Chianti Classico or Soave Classico. Longer ageing is Riserva, higher alcohol is Superiore, a named vineyard is Vigna.

questions.q: Which Italian wine was the first to receive DOC status, in 1966?
questions.exp: Vernaccia di San Gimignano, the Tuscan white, was the first DOC granted under the 1963 law, in 1966; it later became Tuscany's only white DOCG.

questions.q: What is the Italian label word for the sweetness level between Abboccato and Dolce?
questions.exp: The scale runs Secco (dry), Abboccato (off-dry), Amabile (medium sweet), Dolce (sweet). Amabile carries more sugar than Abboccato and less than Dolce; the words appear on Lambrusco, Moscato and Vin Santo labels.

questions.q: Which Super Tuscan holds its own DOC within Bolgheri?
questions.exp: Sassicaia is the only single estate wine in Italy with its own denomination, Bolgheri Sassicaia DOC. Tignanello and Solaia are IGT Toscana; Ornellaia is Bolgheri Superiore DOC.

questions.q: Which grape makes Vino Nobile di Montepulciano?
questions.exp: Vino Nobile is Sangiovese, locally called Prugnolo Gentile, from the Tuscan town of Montepulciano; the Montepulciano grape belongs to Abruzzo and has no part in it.

questions.q: Which Italian sparkling wine is bottle fermented by the traditional method?
questions.exp: Franciacorta takes its second fermentation in the bottle, like Champagne. Prosecco, Moscato d'Asti and Lambrusco are tank wines made to keep fruit and aroma.

regions.name: Piedmont
regions.summary: Piedmont sits in Italy's north-west corner, hemmed in by the Alps and the Apennines, with no coast and no IGT. Nebbiolo is the grape the exam cares about: it makes Barolo and Barbaresco in the Langhe hills around Alba, pale garnet wines with tar, rose, high acid and heavy tannin, each DOCG defined by its ageing minimums. Barbera is the everyday red, Dolcetto the early one, Moscato Bianco the sweet fizz of Asti, Cortese the white of Gavi, Arneis that of Roero. Autumn fog, the nebbia, names the grape; the Tanaro divides Langhe from Roero; the age of the marl divides perfume from power.

terroir.climate: Continental and sheltered: the Alps to the north and west block Atlantic weather and the Apennines close the south, so winters are cold, summers hot and dry, and autumns long, still and foggy. Nebbiolo needs that long tail; it is picked in October, weeks after Dolcetto and Barbera.
terroir.soils: The Langhe is marine marl laid down when this was sea floor. Around La Morra and the village of Barolo the Tortonian marls are bluish, calcareous and fertile, giving perfume and softer tannin. Around Serralunga, Monforte and Castiglione Falletto the older Serravallian formations carry more sandstone and compacted sand, giving denser, longer-lived wine. Roero across the Tanaro is sand; Alto Piemonte is volcanic porphyry and glacial moraine; Gavi is clay over limestone.
terroir.topography: Hill country throughout. Barolo's vineyards sit between roughly 200 and 500 metres on steep slopes south-west of Alba; Barbaresco lies lower and a little warmer to the north-east, so it ripens earlier. The best Nebbiolo sites are the south and south-west facing amphitheatres the Langhe calls sorì. Monferrato rolls lower and softer to the east around Asti; Alto Piemonte climbs towards Monte Rosa.
terroir.water: The Tanaro runs past Alba, the Langhe on its right bank and the Roero on its left; the Po drains the region eastward. No sea or lake moderates the climate, so fog settles in the valleys each autumn.

grapes.name: Nebbiolo
grapes.styles: Barolo and Barbaresco in the Langhe, Roero across the river, and the lighter alpine wines of Gattinara, Ghemme and Carema, where it goes by Spanna or Picotendro. Pale colour, tar and rose, high acid and among the firmest tannins in Italy.

grapes.name: Barbera
grapes.styles: The most planted red of the region and its daily glass: deep colour, high acid, low tannin, sour cherry. Barbera d'Asti and Nizza are the serious DOCGs, Barbera d'Alba the plusher Langhe version.

grapes.name: Dolcetto
grapes.styles: The early-ripening, soft, dry red that takes the cooler sites Nebbiolo refuses; Dogliani and Diano d'Alba give it DOCG status, Dolcetto d'Alba the everyday bottle.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc
grapes.styles: Moscato Bianco makes Moscato d'Asti, gently frizzante and sweet near five per cent alcohol, and the fully sparkling Asti; Canelli is the historic heart and since 2023 its own DOCG.

grapes.name: Cortese
grapes.styles: The white of Gavi in the south-east: lean, citrus, mineral, dry and unoaked, built for the seafood of the Ligurian coast next door.

grapes.name: Arneis
grapes.styles: Roero's white, rescued from near extinction in the 1970s: pear, white flowers, soft acid and a faint bitterness on the finish.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: With Pinot Nero, the base of Alta Langa, the region's traditional method sparkling DOCG, and of some oaked Langhe whites.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Pinot Nero partners Chardonnay in Alta Langa and appears in a few cool Langhe DOC reds.

grapes.name: Brachetto
grapes.styles: A sweet, aromatic, frothy red from Acqui: strawberry and rose, low alcohol, the region's answer to a bowl of berries.

grapes.name: Grignolino
grapes.styles: Pale, tannic and peppery red of Monferrato and Asti, an old local taste served cool.

grapes.name: Freisa
grapes.styles: A relative of Nebbiolo making strawberry-scented, tannic reds, still or lightly fizzy, around Asti and Chieri.

grapes.name: Ruchè
grapes.styles: An aromatic red of Castagnole Monferrato, rose and spice, with its own DOCG since 2010.

grapes.name: Erbaluce
grapes.styles: Canavese's high-acid white, made dry, sparkling or dried for Caluso Passito.

grapes.name: Timorasso
grapes.styles: The Colli Tortonesi white revived from a handful of vines: full, waxy, long-lived, often labelled Derthona.

wines.note: Pale garnet, tar, dried rose, liquorice and truffle over high acid and grippy tannin; it needs years and a big glass. Decant, serve near 17 degrees, with braised beef, truffle dishes or aged cheese.
Nebbiolo from lower, warmer hills north-east of Alba: the same aromatics in a slightly gentler frame with an earlier window. Roast game birds and mushroom risotto suit it.
Bright violet colour, sour cherry and plum, acid high enough to cut through tomato sauce, pork and salumi; little tannin, so it can be served slightly cool.
Soft, dark, dry, with blackberry and bitter almond; the first red opened on a Piedmontese table, drunk young and often.
Cortese: dry, light, lemon and green apple with a stony finish; served cold with raw fish and shellfish.
Pear, chamomile and almond with moderate acid; a rounder white than Gavi for antipasti and vitello tonnato.
Gently frizzante, sweet, grapey and floral at around five per cent alcohol; served cold with fruit, panettone or hazelnut cake, or on its own. Asti is its fully sparkling sibling.
Alto Piemonte Nebbiolo from volcanic soil: lighter in body, higher in acid, with iron and dried flowers; earlier to drink than Barolo.
Traditional method, Pinot Nero and Chardonnay, always vintage dated with at least thirty months on the lees: toasty, dry and serious.
Barolo infused with quinine bark, spices and sugar: a bitter-sweet digestivo poured in small glasses with dark chocolate.

made.viticulture: Nebbiolo buds early and ripens late, so it takes the warmest, best-drained south-facing slopes and everything else takes the cooler aspects: Dolcetto the higher or north-facing sites, Barbera the mid slopes, Moscato the chalky hills around Canelli. Vines are mostly Guyot trained, and the hills are largely picked by hand on slopes too steep for machines. Frost at budbreak, summer hail and rain during the long Nebbiolo harvest are the hazards; Barolo growers watch the sky through October while Dolcetto is already in the cellar. Barolo's rules cap the crop at eight tonnes per hectare and keep Nebbiolo to the hillsides. The MGA system, mapped in Barbaresco in 2007 and Barolo in 2010, lets a bottle name its vineyard, so single-site farming has grown. In Carema, terraces and pergolas on stone pillars lift the vines off the cold ground.
made.winemaking: The old way: long macerations of several weeks, sometimes under a submerged cap, then years in large Slavonian oak botti that let the wine breathe without tasting of wood. The modern way, which arrived in the 1980s: shorter, warmer macerations, rotary fermenters, and ageing in French barriques for colour, softness and earlier appeal. Most houses now sit between the two. The law sets the floor: Barolo must age 38 months from the November after harvest, 18 of them in wood, 62 months for Riserva; Barbaresco 26 months with 9 in wood, 50 for Riserva. Barbera is often given barrique to tame its acid; Dolcetto is kept fresh in steel. Moscato d'Asti is a tank wine whose single fermentation is stopped by chilling and filtration with sugar still in it, which is why it is so low in alcohol. Barolo Chinato infuses finished Barolo with china bark, sugar and spices.

law.classification: Piedmont has no IGT; every bottle is DOCG, DOC or plain vino, and the region holds more DOCGs than any other. The ladder reads from the broad Piemonte DOC, through Langhe and Monferrato DOC, to village denominations and the DOCGs. Barolo and Barbaresco are the model: a single grape, a mapped zone of named communes, ageing minimums counted from the first of November after harvest, and since 2007 and 2010 the Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive, the official vineyard names a label may add: 181 in Barolo (170 vineyards plus the eleven communes), 66 in Barbaresco. Riserva means longer ageing, Superiore higher alcohol, Vigna a named site inside an MGA held to a lower yield.

places.name: Langhe
places.note: The hills south of the Tanaro around Alba, home to Barolo, Barbaresco and the white truffle. Langhe DOC is the broad net (Langhe Nebbiolo, Langhe Chardonnay); Dogliani and Diano d'Alba are its Dolcetto DOCGs.

places.name: Barolo
places.note: Eleven communes south-west of Alba, five of which hold most of the vineyard: La Morra and Barolo on the softer Tortonian marl to the west, Castiglione Falletto, Serralunga d'Alba and Monforte d'Alba on the harder Serravallian ground to the east. All Nebbiolo, 38 months with 18 in wood, 13% minimum.

places.name: La Morra
places.note: The largest commune and the most perfumed Barolo, on Tortonian marl: Brunate (shared with Barolo village), Cerequio, Rocche dell'Annunziata, Arborina.

places.name: Barolo (village)
places.note: The commune that names the wine: Cannubi, the most famous hill, with Sarmassa and lower Brunate.

places.name: Castiglione Falletto
places.note: Both soils meet in the centre of the zone: Monprivato, Villero, Rocche di Castiglione, Bricco Boschis.

places.name: Serralunga d'Alba
places.note: The eastern ridge on Serravallian sandstone and marl, the most tannic and longest-lived Barolo: Vigna Rionda, Francia, Lazzarito, Falletto.

places.name: Monforte d'Alba
places.note: The south-east, powerful and dark: Bussia, Ginestra, Mosconi, Santo Stefano di Perno.

places.name: Barbaresco
places.note: Three communes north-east of Alba, Barbaresco, Neive and Treiso, plus a sliver of Alba itself. Lower, nearer the Tanaro and mostly on Tortonian soils, so the Nebbiolo ripens a week or two earlier and the wine opens sooner: 26 months with 9 in wood, 12.5% minimum.

places.name: Barbaresco (village)
places.note: Asili, Rabajà, Martinenga, Montestefano and Pora, with the Gaja house's Sorì Tildìn and Sorì San Lorenzo.

places.name: Neive
places.note: Fuller, more structured Barbaresco from the north-east: Santo Stefano, Gallina, Basarin, Currà.

places.name: Treiso
places.note: The highest and coolest of the three, the most delicate wines: Pajorè, Bernadot, Marcarini.

places.name: Dogliani
places.note: The Dolcetto DOCG south of Barolo, where the grape is taken seriously enough to age a few years.

places.name: Alba
places.note: The town at the centre of the Langhe; Nebbiolo d'Alba, Barbera d'Alba and Dolcetto d'Alba cover the wider hills and Roero.

places.name: Roero
places.note: The left bank of the Tanaro north of Alba, sand over marl, steeper and more eroded than the Langhe. DOCG since 2004 for Roero (lighter, earlier Nebbiolo) and Roero Arneis.

places.name: Monferrato
places.note: The rolling hills east of the Langhe between Asti and Casale, Barbera's homeland: Barbera d'Asti DOCG, Barbera del Monferrato, Grignolino, Freisa and Ruchè di Castagnole Monferrato, with the Moscato hills around Canelli.

places.name: Asti and Canelli
places.note: Asti DOCG covers both the fully sparkling Asti and the frizzante Moscato d'Asti; Canelli is the cellar town of the sparkling trade and since 2023 a Moscato DOCG in its own name.

places.name: Nizza
places.note: All Barbera from Nizza Monferrato and its neighbours, carved out of Barbera d'Asti as its own DOCG in 2014, with longer ageing.

places.name: Acqui
places.note: Brachetto d'Acqui DOCG, the sweet sparkling red, and Dolcetto d'Acqui; the spa town lies south-east towards Liguria.

places.name: Gavi
places.note: The south-eastern corner near the Ligurian border, limestone and clay, where Cortese makes the dry white Gavi, DOCG since 1998. Gavi di Gavi means fruit from the commune of Gavi itself.

places.name: Alto Piemonte
places.note: The hills north of Novara and Vercelli below Monte Rosa, on volcanic porphyry and glacial moraine. Nebbiolo is Spanna here, blended with Vespolina and Uva Rara into lighter, high-acid, mineral reds; Lessona, Bramaterra, Boca, Fara and Sizzano are the DOCs of the revival.

places.name: Gattinara
places.note: DOCG since 1990: at least 90% Nebbiolo, 35 months' ageing, from the hills above the town.

places.name: Ghemme
places.note: DOCG since 1997 across the Sesia in the province of Novara: at least 85% Nebbiolo, 34 months' ageing.

places.name: Canavese and Carema
places.note: North of Turin at the mouth of the Aosta valley: Carema DOC trains Nebbiolo, here Picotendro, on pergolas over stone pillars; Erbaluce di Caluso DOCG makes dry, sparkling and passito whites.

places.name: Colli Tortonesi
places.note: Hills around Tortona in the far east, where Timorasso was revived; the wine is often sold as Derthona, the town's Roman name.

places.name: Alta Langa
places.note: The high hills south of the Langhe above 250 metres, DOCG since 2011 for traditional method sparkling from Pinot Nero and Chardonnay, vintage only, at least 30 months on the lees.

producers.name: Gaja
producers.why: The Barbaresco house, founded 1859, that took Piedmont to the world market with single-vineyard bottlings and barrique; Sorì Tildìn and Sorì San Lorenzo are its names.

producers.name: Bruno Giacosa
producers.why: Neive house famed for a classic hand in both Barbaresco (Santo Stefano, Asili) and Barolo (Falletto); the red label marks its Riserva.

producers.name: Giacomo Conterno
producers.why: Monforte's keeper of the traditional school; Monfortino Riserva is the longest-aged and most sought-after Barolo.

producers.name: Bartolo Mascarello
producers.why: Barolo village traditionalist blending four vineyards into one wine in large old casks: no barrique, no single-vineyard labels.

producers.name: Giuseppe Rinaldi
producers.why: Another Barolo village traditionalist, long macerations and blended crus; Brunate and Tre Tine.

producers.name: Produttori del Barbaresco
producers.why: The village cooperative of Barbaresco, founded 1958, a benchmark for price and purity, with single-vineyard Riserve in good years.

producers.name: Vietti
producers.why: Castiglione Falletto house that pioneered single-vineyard Barolo in the 1960s and replanted Arneis; Rocche di Castiglione, Lazzarito, Ravera.

producers.name: G.D. Vajra
producers.why: The highest vineyards of Barolo commune at Vergne; Bricco delle Viole, plus a rare Freisa and a Riesling.

producers.name: Luciano Sandrone
producers.why: Modern-leaning Barolo from Cannubi Boschis, now labelled Aleste, and the blended Le Vigne.

producers.name: Giuseppe Mascarello e Figlio
producers.why: Monprivato in Castiglione Falletto, a near monopole and one of the great traditional single-vineyard Barolos.

producers.name: Cappellano
producers.why: Serralunga house that created Barolo Chinato in the late nineteenth century and still farms a plot of ungrafted Nebbiolo.

producers.name: Poderi Aldo Conterno
producers.why: Monforte house on the Bussia hill: Granbussia Riserva, Cicala, Colonnello and Romirasco.

producers.name: Massolino
producers.why: Serralunga's Vigna Rionda Riserva, classical and long-lived.

producers.name: Cavallotto
producers.why: Castiglione Falletto's Bricco Boschis, a monopole farmed organically with long cask ageing.

producers.name: Fontanafredda
producers.why: The historic Serralunga estate on land bought in 1858 by Vittorio Emanuele II, the king who went on to unite Italy; long the largest single Barolo estate.

producers.name: Pio Cesare
producers.why: Alba merchant house founded 1881 with cellars inside the town's Roman walls, blending across Barolo and Barbaresco.

producers.name: Renato Ratti
producers.why: La Morra house whose founder drew the first map of Barolo's crus in the 1970s; Marcenasco.

producers.name: Domenico Clerico
producers.why: Monforte modernist of the 1980s; Ciabot Mentin from the Ginestra hill.

producers.name: Roagna
producers.why: Barbaresco traditionalist with old vines, very long macerations and late releases; Pajè.

producers.name: Marchesi di Grésy
producers.why: Owner of the whole Martinenga amphitheatre in Barbaresco, a monopole.

producers.name: La Spinetta
producers.why: Moscato roots in Castagnole Lanze, then modern Barbaresco and Barolo under the rhinoceros label.

producers.name: Braida
producers.why: The Monferrato house that put Barbera in barrique with Bricco dell'Uccellone in 1982 and made the grape serious.

producers.name: La Miraja
producers.why: Castagnole Monferrato estate for Barbera d'Asti and the aromatic Ruchè.

producers.name: La Scolca
producers.why: The Gavi house whose black label Gavi dei Gavi made Cortese famous.

producers.name: Saracco
producers.why: Castiglione Tinella grower house regarded as the reference for Moscato d'Asti.

producers.name: Antoniolo
producers.why: Gattinara's leading estate, single-vineyard Spanna from Osso San Grato and San Francesco.

producers.name: Travaglini
producers.why: Gattinara house known for its bent bottle and long-aged Riserva.

producers.name: Proprietà Sperino
producers.why: The estate that revived Lessona and with it Alto Piemonte's reputation.

exam: Barolo and Barbaresco: all Nebbiolo, the ageing minimums (38 and 26 months, 18 and 9 in wood), the Riserva minimums (62 and 50), and where each lies relative to Alba.
The five core Barolo communes and the Tortonian versus Serravallian split; the three Barbaresco communes.
Nebbiolo's synonyms by place: Spanna, Chiavennasca, Picotendro.
The grape behind each place name: Gavi is Cortese, Roero's white is Arneis, Asti and Moscato d'Asti are Moscato Bianco, Nizza is Barbera, Dogliani is Dolcetto, Acqui is Brachetto.
Moscato d'Asti: tank method, stopped fermentation, around five per cent alcohol, frizzante not spumante.
Alta Langa as Piedmont's traditional method DOCG, vintage only.
Piedmont has no IGT; the MGA system and the year each zone adopted it.
traps: Nebbiolo looks light in the glass; it is not light in the mouth. Pale garnet with high acid and high tannin is the tell.
Barbaresco is not a lesser Barolo; it is the same grape from lower, earlier-ripening hills with shorter minimums.
Barbera has high acid and low tannin; Dolcetto has low acid and moderate tannin; Nebbiolo has both high. Do not swap them.
Asti is the fully sparkling wine; Moscato d'Asti is frizzante and lower in alcohol. Both are Moscato Bianco, neither is Muscat of Alexandria.
Gavi is a town and Cortese its grape; Dolcetto means little sweet one but the wine is dry.
The Tanaro: Langhe on the right bank, Roero on the left; Barbaresco is north-east of Alba, Barolo south-west.
Gattinara and Ghemme are Nebbiolo DOCGs of Alto Piemonte, not of the Langhe, and the grape there may be blended.
The old course note called the climate simply continental; add the autumn fog and the Alpine shelter, which are what make the harvest so late.

cards.b: All Nebbiolo; 38 months from 1 November after harvest, 18 in wood; Riserva 62 months. Minimum 13% alcohol.
All Nebbiolo; 26 months, 9 in wood; Riserva 50 months. 12.5% minimum. North-east of Alba, lower and earlier than Barolo.
Tortonian marl (La Morra, Barolo village): softer, perfumed, earlier. Serravallian sandstone and compact marl (Serralunga, Monforte, Castiglione Falletto): denser, more tannic, longer-lived.
Spanna in Alto Piemonte (Gattinara, Ghemme), Chiavennasca in Valtellina, Picotendro in Carema and the Aosta valley.

cards.f: Grape behind Gavi, Roero's white, Asti, Nizza, Dogliani, Acqui
cards.b: Gavi: Cortese. Roero: Arneis. Asti and Moscato d'Asti: Moscato Bianco. Nizza: Barbera. Dogliani: Dolcetto. Brachetto d'Acqui: Brachetto.
Both Moscato Bianco, both tank method. Moscato d'Asti is frizzante, sweet, near 5 to 5.5% alcohol; Asti is fully sparkling, usually sweet and stronger, with a dry Asti Secco allowed since 2017.
Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive, the official vineyard names a label may carry: Barbaresco from 2007 (66), Barolo from 2010 (181, including the eleven communes).

cards.f: Barolo's communes: how many, which matter
cards.b: Eleven in all; the five that matter: La Morra, Barolo, Castiglione Falletto, Serralunga d'Alba, Monforte d'Alba. Also Novello, Verduno, Grinzane Cavour, Diano d'Alba, Roddi, Cherasco.
Piedmont's traditional method sparkling: Pinot Nero and Chardonnay, vintage only, at least 30 months on the lees, from hills above 250 metres.
None. Piedmont, with the Valle d'Aosta next door, is one of the two Italian regions with no IGT; its wines are DOCG, DOC or plain vino.

questions.q: What is the minimum total ageing for Barolo before release?
questions.exp: Barolo ages at least 38 months from 1 November after harvest, 18 in wood. Barbaresco takes 26, Barbaresco Riserva 50 and Barolo Riserva 62.

questions.q: Which Barolo commune sits on the harder Serravallian soils and makes the most tannic, longest-lived wines?
questions.exp: Serralunga's eastern ridge is Serravallian sandstone and compact marl. La Morra is Tortonian and perfumed; Castiglione Falletto mixes the two; Grinzane Cavour is a minor commune.

questions.q: Which river divides the Langhe from the Roero?
questions.exp: The Tanaro runs past Alba with the Langhe on its right bank and the sandy Roero on its left. The Po drains Piedmont eastward; the Adige and Ticino are elsewhere.

questions.q: Name the grape of Gavi.
questions.exp: Gavi is a town in south-east Piedmont; its dry white is all Cortese, DOCG since 1998 under the names Gavi or Cortese di Gavi.

questions.q: What is Nebbiolo called in Gattinara and Ghemme?
questions.exp: In Alto Piemonte the grape is Spanna; in Valtellina it is Chiavennasca and in Carema Picotendro. Same vine, alpine editions.

questions.q: Which Piedmont DOCG is a traditional method sparkling wine from Pinot Nero and Chardonnay?
questions.exp: Alta Langa is bottle fermented, vintage only, with at least 30 months on the lees. Asti and Brachetto d'Acqui are sweet tank wines; Erbaluce di Caluso is a white DOCG that includes a sparkling style.

questions.q: In which year did Barolo adopt its official list of vineyard names, the MGA?
questions.exp: Barolo mapped its Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive in 2010; Barbaresco did so in 2007. Roero became DOCG in 2004 and Nizza in 2014.

questions.q: Which white grape shares the Roero DOCG with Nebbiolo?
questions.exp: Roero DOCG covers both a Nebbiolo red and the white Roero Arneis, a grape all but lost by the 1970s and replanted on the sandy left bank of the Tanaro.

regions.name: Lombardy
regions.summary: Lombardy is Milan's hinterland, and its wine is sorted by altitude and water rather than by one great grape. Franciacorta, on glacial moraine south of Lake Iseo, is the country's benchmark traditional method sparkling wine, Chardonnay with Pinot Nero and Pinot Bianco. Valtellina terraces Nebbiolo, called Chiavennasca here, on the sunny north bank of the Adda in an alpine valley, and dries it for Sforzato. Lugana makes a fresh white from Turbiana on the south shore of Garda, and Oltrepò Pavese, across the Po, holds the largest planting of Pinot Nero in Italy. Lakes, not sea, do the moderating.

terroir.climate: Three climates in one region. The Po plain is humid, foggy in winter and hot in summer. The lakes (Garda, Iseo, Como) store heat and soften the extremes on their shores, which is what Franciacorta and Lugana depend on. Valtellina is alpine and continental, dry, with strong sun on its south-facing wall and a sharp drop at night; the breva, a daytime breeze off Lake Como, dries the vines.
terroir.soils: Franciacorta sits on the moraine left by the Iseo glacier: deep gravel and sand mixed with limestone pebbles, free draining and warm. Valtellina's terraces are shallow, sandy, acidic soils weathered from granite and schist, held by dry stone walls. Lugana is heavy white clay of glacial origin, which gives its white weight and keeps it fresh. Oltrepò Pavese is clay and limestone in the Apennine foothills.
terroir.topography: From the Alps in the north through the lake district to the flat Po plain, then the Apennine foothills of Oltrepò across the river in the south. Franciacorta is a low amphitheatre of hills below Lake Iseo; Valtellina is an east-west valley whose north bank faces due south, terraced from the valley floor to around 700 metres; Lugana is nearly flat.
terroir.water: The Po crosses the whole south of the region; the Adda runs through Valtellina and into Lake Como; Lake Iseo warms Franciacorta and Lake Garda warms Lugana and the Valtènesi shore. Lakes rather than sea are the moderating water here.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The backbone of Franciacorta and the larger part of its Satèn, beside Pinot Bianco; also still Curtefranca Bianco.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Pinot Nero: Franciacorta's structure and the required core of its Rosé; the base of Oltrepò Pavese's traditional method sparkling and the most planted Pinot Nero in Italy, also made still.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Pinot Bianco, up to half of a Franciacorta and a partner in Satèn.

grapes.name: Nebbiolo
grapes.styles: Chiavennasca in Valtellina: lighter, more floral and more acid than Barolo, grown on terraces; dried for Sforzato.

grapes.name: Turbiana
grapes.styles: Lugana's grape, once labelled Trebbiano di Lugana and now known to be Verdicchio: citrus, almond, a saline edge, and the ability to age.

grapes.name: Croatina
grapes.styles: Oltrepò's dark, soft red, sold as Bonarda dell'Oltrepò Pavese, often frizzante.

grapes.name: Groppello
grapes.styles: The local red of the Valtènesi on Garda's western shore, made into the pale Chiaretto rosé.

grapes.name: Erbamat
grapes.styles: An old Brescian white, high in acid and late ripening, admitted to Franciacorta from 2017 at up to ten per cent.

grapes.name: Moscato di Scanzo
grapes.styles: A red Moscato near Bergamo making a sweet passito with Italy's smallest DOCG.

grapes.name: Lambrusco
grapes.styles: Lambrusco Mantovano around Mantua, the Lombard end of the Emilian frizzante tradition.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Oltrepò Pavese grows both Riesling Renano and Riesling Italico, which is Welschriesling, for dry whites.

wines.note: Traditional method, dry, fine mousse, apple and brioche, at least eighteen months on the lees for the basic wine; served as Champagne is, well chilled in a tall glass, with anything fried or salted.
White grapes only, lower pressure, always Brut: a silkier, softer mousse. The name was coined by the consortium and belongs to it.
Pinot Nero gives a substantial share of the blend; 24 months on the lees; red fruit and a firmer line.
At least 90% Nebbiolo with two years' ageing, from the terraced subzones: pale, floral, red fruit, firm acid and tannin, lighter than Barolo and ready sooner.
Nebbiolo dried after harvest, then fermented dry to at least 14%; the first dry dried-grape red to be DOCG, with Nebbiolo's perfume over Amarone's weight.
Turbiana: dry, medium bodied, citrus and almond with a saline edge, served cold with the lake's fish and risotto.
At least 70% Pinot Nero, bottle fermented; with Franciacorta and Alta Langa, one of Italy's traditional method DOCGs.
Croatina, soft and dark, often lightly frizzante, the carafe wine of Pavia with salami.
Groppello-led, pale, dry rosé from Garda's western shore, for lake fish and summer.
A tiny sweet red passito from a hamlet near Bergamo, rose and spice; Italy's smallest DOCG.

made.viticulture: Franciacorta is farmed for sparkling wine: Chardonnay and Pinot Nero picked early and by hand (hand harvest is compulsory), yields capped, Guyot and spur-pruned cordon on the moraine. The mild lake climate makes ripeness easy, so the task is keeping acidity. Valtellina is the opposite: heroic viticulture on terraces too narrow for anything but hands and, in places, a small helicopter for the crates; the dry stone walls store the day's heat, the slope faces due south, and the grapes for Sforzato are laid in airy lofts to dry through the autumn until a good part of their weight has gone. Lugana's clay and Garda's mild air allow machine work on flat ground. Oltrepò Pavese is hill country of Pinot Nero, Croatina and Barbera, farmed by cooperatives and estates alike. Hazards: hail and summer storms on the plain, frost and landslip in the valley.
made.winemaking: Franciacorta follows the Champagne sequence: gentle pressing, base wines fermented in steel or some oak, assemblage, second fermentation in the bottle of sale, lees ageing well beyond the legal floor (18 months non vintage, 24 for Satèn and Rosé, 30 for vintage, 60 for Riserva), riddling, disgorgement and dosage from Pas Dosé to Demi-Sec. Satèn is bottled to a lower pressure, under five atmospheres, and only as Brut. The law lets the name Franciacorta stand alone on the label without the words spumante or DOCG. Valtellina Superiore ages at least 24 months with 12 in wood; Sforzato takes dried grapes to a dry wine of 14% or more and ages at least 20 months. Lugana is cold fermented in steel, sometimes with lees stirring; Riserva and late-harvest versions exist. Oltrepò's Bonarda is often fermented in pressurised tank for its gentle fizz, and its Pinot Nero goes both into bottle-fermented sparkling and into still red.

law.classification: Franciacorta DOCG (1995) was the first Italian denomination reserved for bottle-fermented sparkling wine, and it is the model: Chardonnay, Pinot Nero and Pinot Bianco (the last capped at half), with Erbamat allowed up to ten per cent since 2017; styles are defined by lees time and grape (Satèn, Rosé, Millesimato, Riserva); still wines from the same hills are Curtefranca DOC. Valtellina Superiore DOCG (1998) names five subzones and demands 90% Nebbiolo; Sforzato di Valtellina DOCG (2003) is the dried-grape red; Rosso di Valtellina DOC is the lighter wine. Oltrepò Pavese Metodo Classico DOCG (2007) covers Pinot Nero-led traditional method sparkling, while the Oltrepò's still wines stay DOC. Lugana DOC straddles the border with Veneto. Moscato di Scanzo DOCG is the smallest in the country. Lombardy, unlike Piedmont, has IGTs for everything else.

DOC
Curtefranca, Rosso di Valtellina, Lugana, Oltrepò Pavese, Riviera del Garda Classico, Garda, San Colombano, Lambrusco Mantovano among others

labels: Franciacorta from white grapes only, under five atmospheres, Brut dosage, 24 months on the lees
Vintage Franciacorta: at least 85% from the stated year, 30 months on the lees
Vintage dated, at least 60 months on the lees
No sugar added at disgorgement; the driest dosage
Valtellina Nebbiolo from dried grapes, dry, 14% minimum
The pale rosé of Garda's shores

places.name: Franciacorta
places.note: The hills south of Lake Iseo in the province of Brescia; Erbusco is the main village. Traditional method sparkling since 1961, when the first bottles were made at Berlucchi, then DOC in 1967 and DOCG in 1995.

places.name: Valtellina
places.note: The alpine valley of the Adda north of Lake Como, terraced on its south-facing north bank around Sondrio. Five subzones of Valtellina Superiore run west to east: Maroggia, Sassella, Grumello, Inferno, Valgella.

places.name: Sassella
places.note: The steepest and most famous subzone, just west of Sondrio, named for a chapel on the rock.

places.name: Grumello
places.note: Beside the castle east of Sondrio; rounder wines than Sassella.

places.name: Inferno
places.note: The hottest pocket of the valley, named for the heat caught between its rocks; the firmest wines.

places.name: Valgella
places.note: The largest and easternmost subzone, lighter and earlier.

places.name: Maroggia
places.note: The smallest and westernmost, recognised as a subzone in 2002.

places.name: Lugana
places.note: The south shore of Garda around Sirmione and Peschiera, mostly in Lombardy with a strip in Veneto, white clay, Turbiana; the one Garda white with a serious reputation.

places.name: Oltrepò Pavese
places.note: The hills south of Pavia across the Po, the Apennine foothills, the region's largest vineyard: Pinot Nero still and sparkling, Croatina as Bonarda, Barbera, Riesling; Buttafuoco and Sangue di Giuda are its local red styles.

places.name: Valtènesi and the Garda shore
places.note: Garda's western shore in the Riviera del Garda Classico DOC: Groppello and the Chiaretto rosé.

places.name: Moscato di Scanzo
places.note: A hamlet above Bergamo; a red Moscato dried for a sweet wine; Italy's smallest DOCG, granted in 2009.

places.name: San Colombano
places.note: The one hill in the province of Milan with a DOC, near Lodi.

places.name: Lambrusco Mantovano
places.note: Lambrusco around Mantua on the Po, the Lombard end of the Emilian fizz.

producers.name: Ca' del Bosco
producers.why: Erbusco house whose Cuvée Annamaria Clementi Riserva is Franciacorta's reference prestige cuvée.

producers.name: Bellavista
producers.why: Erbusco's other leading house, long-aged vintage Franciacorta and the Gran Cuvée.

producers.name: Berlucchi
producers.why: Where Franciacorta began: the first bottle-fermented wine from these hills, in 1961.

producers.name: Cavalleri
producers.why: An Erbusco grower-house with a reputation for Blanc de Blancs Franciacorta.

producers.name: Barone Pizzini
producers.why: An early adopter of organic farming in Franciacorta.

producers.name: Ar.Pe.Pe.
producers.why: Valtellina's traditionalist: very long-aged Sassella and Grumello Riserve in large casks.

producers.name: Nino Negri
producers.why: Founded 1897 in Chiuro, long the valley's largest house; its 5 Stelle Sfursat is the reference Sforzato.

producers.name: Rainoldi
producers.why: Chiuro house for Inferno and Sassella Riserva.

producers.name: Ca' dei Frati
producers.why: Lugana's best-known estate: I Frati and the aged Brolettino.

producers.name: Conte Vistarino
producers.why: The Oltrepò Pavese estate that planted Pinot Nero in the nineteenth century and makes still Pinot Nero crus.

exam: Franciacorta: traditional method, the three grapes plus Erbamat, the lees minimums by style, Satèn's definition.
Prosecco versus Franciacorta: tank versus bottle, Glera versus Chardonnay and Pinot Nero.
Valtellina: Nebbiolo as Chiavennasca, the five subzones, Sforzato as a dried-grape dry red.
Lugana: Turbiana, the Garda shore shared with Veneto.
Oltrepò Pavese as Pinot Nero country and a traditional method DOCG.
Which Lombard DOCG is Italy's smallest: Moscato di Scanzo.
traps: Satèn is not a sweetness level; it is a white-grape Franciacorta at lower pressure, always Brut.
Franciacorta is one of the few Italian names allowed to stand alone on the label without spumante or DOCG; do not read that as a lower tier.
Sforzato is dry; it is not Recioto and not sweet. It is Valtellina's Amarone, made from Nebbiolo, not Corvina.
Chiavennasca is Nebbiolo; the town is Chiavenna but the wine zone is Valtellina.
Lugana's grape was called Trebbiano di Lugana but it is Verdicchio, not the Trebbiano Toscano of Tuscany.
Bonarda in Oltrepò is Croatina; Bonarda in Alto Piemonte is Uva Rara; Argentina's Bonarda is a different grape again.
Inferno is a Valtellina subzone, not a style; the name is about heat on the slope.

cards.b: Chardonnay, Pinot Nero, Pinot Bianco (max 50%), Erbamat up to 10% since 2017. Traditional method, second fermentation in bottle. DOCG 1995, the first Italian DOCG reserved for bottle-fermented sparkling wine.
Non vintage 18 months; Satèn and Rosé 24; Millesimato 30; Riserva 60 (vintage dated).
Franciacorta from white grapes only (Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco), bottled under 5 atmospheres for a softer mousse, always Brut, 24 months on lees.
Nebbiolo (Chiavennasca) 90% minimum, 24 months' ageing with 12 in wood. West to east: Maroggia, Sassella, Grumello, Inferno, Valgella.
Dried-grape Nebbiolo fermented dry, 14% minimum, DOCG 2003; also spelt Sfursat. Lombardy's answer to Amarone.
Turbiana (once Trebbiano di Lugana, genetically Verdicchio), on white clay at the south end of Lake Garda, mostly Lombardy, partly Veneto.
Hills south of the Po near Pavia; Italy's largest Pinot Nero planting; Oltrepò Pavese Metodo Classico DOCG (70% Pinot Nero minimum); Bonarda here means Croatina.
Moscato di Scanzo, a sweet red passito from a hamlet near Bergamo, Lombardy, DOCG since 2009.

questions.q: Which lake lies immediately north of the Franciacorta hills?
questions.exp: Franciacorta sits on the moraine left by the Iseo glacier, south of Lake Iseo near Brescia. Garda warms Lugana, Como sits below Valtellina, Maggiore is on the Piedmont border.

questions.q: What is the minimum time on the lees for a non-vintage Franciacorta?
questions.exp: The basic Franciacorta needs 18 months on the lees; Satèn and Rosé need 24, Millesimato 30 and Riserva 60.

questions.q: Under what name does Nebbiolo grow in Valtellina?
questions.exp: Chiavennasca is Valtellina's name for Nebbiolo. Spanna is the Alto Piemonte name, Picotendro the Carema and Aosta name, Prunent the Ossola valley's.

questions.q: Which grape variety makes the white wine Lugana?
questions.exp: Lugana is Turbiana, long sold as Trebbiano di Lugana and shown by DNA to be the same vine as Verdicchio, grown on white clay at Garda's south end.

questions.q: Name the Franciacorta style made only from white grapes at lower pressure.
questions.exp: Satèn is Chardonnay and Pinot Bianco bottled under five atmospheres, always Brut, with 24 months on the lees; the name is the consortium's own.

questions.q: Which Valtellina wine is made from grapes dried after the harvest and fermented dry?
questions.exp: Sforzato, or Sfursat, dries Chiavennasca after picking and ferments it dry to at least 14%. Valtellina Superiore and Rosso di Valtellina are fresh-grape wines; Sassella is a Superiore subzone.

questions.q: What grape is sold as Bonarda in the Oltrepò Pavese?
questions.exp: In Oltrepò Pavese the wine called Bonarda is made from Croatina, soft, dark and often frizzante; the name Bonarda means other grapes in Piedmont and Argentina.

regions.name: Veneto
regions.summary: Veneto, from the Alps and Lake Garda to Venice, is usually Italy's largest wine region by volume and the home of three wines every server pours: Prosecco, Soave and Valpolicella. Prosecco is Glera made sparkling in tank, with the Conegliano Valdobbiadene and Asolo hills as DOCG above a wide DOC. Soave is Garganega from volcanic and limestone hills east of Verona. Valpolicella is Corvina-led red north of Verona, which dried grapes turn into Amarone (dry) and Recioto (sweet), with Ripasso in between. Garda cools the west, the Adriatic the east, and the plain in the middle grows the volume.

terroir.climate: Warm continental on the plain, moderated by Lake Garda to the west and the Adriatic to the south-east, with the Alps and the pre-Alpine Lessini and Treviso hills blocking the north. Valpolicella's valleys draw cool air down from the Lessini at night; the Prosecco hills are wetter and cooler than the plain; summers are hot and humid enough that mildew and hail are the daily worries.
terroir.soils: Soave Classico is volcanic basalt on the Monteforte side and limestone on the Soave side, two faces that give smoke and stone respectively. Valpolicella's hills are limestone and marl with volcanic patches towards the Valpantena and the east; the plain is alluvial gravel and clay. The Conegliano Valdobbiadene hills are marl, sandstone and moraine on steep, eroded slopes. The Colli Euganei are extinct volcanoes; Custoza and Bardolino sit on glacial moraine left by the Garda glacier.
terroir.topography: A band of pre-Alpine hills along the north, the flat Po and Adige plain to the south and Garda on the western edge. Valpolicella is a fan of parallel valleys (the five Classico communes, then Valpantena, then the eastern valleys) running south out of the Lessini into Verona. Soave and Gambellara sit in the hills east of the city; Conegliano Valdobbiadene and Asolo climb steep hogback ridges north of Treviso, with Cartizze a single sheltered hillside.
terroir.water: Lake Garda, the largest in Italy, moderates Bardolino, Custoza and the western Valpolicella; the Adige flows past Verona; the Piave crosses the Prosecco country; the Venetian lagoon closes the east. Water gives the west its mildness and the east its humidity.

grapes.name: Glera
grapes.styles: The Prosecco grape, itself called Prosecco until 2009: pear, white flowers and green apple, made sparkling in tank to keep that freshness; at least 85% of any Prosecco.

grapes.name: Garganega
grapes.styles: Soave's grape, at least 70% of the blend: lemon, almond and a saline stone, late ripening on pergolas; dried, it makes Recioto di Soave.

grapes.name: Corvina
grapes.styles: The lead of Valpolicella, Amarone and Bardolino: sour cherry, thick skins that dry well, moderate tannin. Corvinone, a separate larger-berried grape, may replace up to half of its share.

grapes.name: Rondinella
grapes.styles: Valpolicella's reliable second grape, 5 to 30%: neutral but disease resistant and good for drying.

grapes.name: Molinara
grapes.styles: Once compulsory in Valpolicella, now optional; pale and high in acid, it lightened the blend.

grapes.name: Oseleta
grapes.styles: A tiny-berried, tannic local red revived for colour and grip in Valpolicella blends.

grapes.name: Trebbiano di Soave
grapes.styles: Soave's permitted partner, genetically Verdicchio; adds acid.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Grown in volume on the plain for Delle Venezie DOC, the three-region Pinot Grigio denomination created in 2017.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Pinot Nero gives Prosecco DOC Rosé its 10 to 15% and its red fruit, a category created in 2020.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Up to 15% in Prosecco and the base of some Lessini sparkling.

grapes.name: Durella
grapes.styles: The searingly acid white of the Lessini hills, made into traditional method Lessini Durello.

grapes.name: Raboso
grapes.styles: A dark, tannic, high-acid red of the Piave plain; Piave Malanotte is its DOCG.

grapes.name: Moscato Giallo
grapes.styles: Fior d'Arancio in the Colli Euganei, sweet sparkling and passito.

grapes.name: Tai
grapes.styles: Friulano's Veneto name since 2007; Lison DOCG shares it with Friuli.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The most planted red on the Venetian plain, for soft everyday wine.

wines.note: Glera, tank method, dry to off-dry, pear and white flowers, light and fresh at around 11%; the DOC is the ocean, the DOCGs the hills. Most is Brut or Extra Dry; serve cold, often in a spritz.
The hill DOCG: finer, more floral, sometimes vintage dated from a single Rive, with Superiore di Cartizze at the peak.
Glera with Pinot Nero, vintage dated, 60 days minimum in tank, Brut Nature to Extra Dry; a category since 2020.
Garganega: dry, light to medium, lemon, pear, almond and a chalky or smoky finish; Classico from the hills ages a decade. Risotto, lake fish, white asparagus.
The fresh red: sour cherry, almond, light tannin, drunk young and cool; Superiore is a year older and a shade more serious.
Valpolicella re-fermented on the skins of Amarone: fuller, rounder, dried-fruit tones, the stepping stone between the two.

Dried grapes fermented dry to 14% at the least and usually 15 or more: black cherry, fig, chocolate, bitter almond, velvet tannin, high alcohol. Serve just below room temperature with braised beef, game or hard aged cheese, never with delicate food.
The sweet ancestor of Amarone: the same dried grapes with fermentation halted, red, lush, for chocolate and blue cheese.
Garganega dried on racks into a golden, honeyed sweet wine; Veneto's first DOCG, in 1998.
Corvina-led, pale and light from Garda's eastern shore, served cool; Chiaretto di Bardolino is its pale rosé.
A blended white from the moraine south of Garda, easy and floral, for an aperitivo.
Durella bottle fermented in the volcanic Lessini hills: sharp, mineral, long on the lees.

made.viticulture: Pergola Veronese, the overhead trellis, is the traditional training of Soave and Valpolicella: it suits Garganega's vigour, shades the fruit in a hot summer and keeps bunches healthy for drying; Guyot has spread for quality still wine. Grapes destined for Amarone and Recioto are chosen in the vineyard, picked early into shallow crates, and must be whole, loose-clustered and sound, because they will spend the autumn in the fruttaio, the drying loft. Prosecco in the DOCG hills is hand picked on slopes so steep the growers call the work heroic, and the Rive bottlings must be hand harvested and vintage dated; the plain is machine picked and high yielding, which keeps the price down. Hazards are hail, downy mildew in humid summers, and rot in the drying lofts if the autumn is damp; the lofts are ventilated and the bunches inspected for the better part of three months.
made.winemaking: Appassimento is the Veneto's method: whole bunches lose around a third of their weight over three to four months, concentrating sugar, acid and glycerol and letting a little botrytis in. Pressed no earlier than December, fermented slowly through the winter to dryness, 14% at the least and usually more, Amarone then ages at least two years (four for Riserva); stopped early with sugar remaining, the same must is Recioto. Ripasso puts finished Valpolicella onto the warm pomace of Amarone or Recioto for a second short fermentation, lifting alcohol and body; the law ties the volume of Ripasso to the Amarone whose skins it uses. Prosecco is made by the Martinotti tank method: second fermentation in sealed pressure tanks, a few weeks on the lees, filtered and bottled under pressure, with sweetness set by residual sugar from Brut Nature to Demi-Sec; col fondo, or sui lieviti, is the old bottle-refermented, cloudy, undisgorged style. Soave is pressed and cold fermented in steel; Classico Riservas see large oak or lees.

law.classification: Veneto's denominations fall into three families. Prosecco is a pyramid: Prosecco DOC across nine provinces of Veneto and Friuli, then two hill DOCGs, Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore and Asolo Prosecco, with the Rive (43 named hamlets, vintage dated, hand picked) and Superiore di Cartizze (one hill in Valdobbiadene) at the top. Valpolicella is a ladder of methods on one blend: Valpolicella DOC (and Superiore), Valpolicella Ripasso DOC (its own DOC since 2010), Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG and Recioto della Valpolicella DOCG (both 2010), each available as Classico from the five historic communes or as Valpantena. Soave DOC has Classico and Colli Scaligeri zones, Soave Superiore DOCG and Recioto di Soave DOCG, and since 2019 33 named UGA, the unità geografiche aggiuntive. Bardolino Superiore, Piave Malanotte, Colli di Conegliano, Lison, Recioto di Gambellara, Montello Rosso, Bagnoli Friularo and Colli Euganei Fior d'Arancio complete the DOCG list.

places.name: Valpolicella
places.note: The valleys north of Verona between the Adige and the Lessini. Corvina 45 to 95% (Corvinone may stand in for up to half of it), Rondinella 5 to 30%, the rest from other local reds. The same blend makes four wines by method: Valpolicella, Ripasso, Amarone and Recioto.

places.name: Valpolicella Classico
places.note: The original five communes to the west: Negrar, Fumane, Marano di Valpolicella, Sant'Ambrogio di Valpolicella and San Pietro in Cariano; the great Amarone houses cluster here.

places.name: Negrar
places.note: The largest of the Classico communes, home of the most famous traditional Amarone cellar and of a large cooperative.

places.name: Fumane
places.note: The valley of the La Grola hill and of the Allegrini house.

places.name: Sant'Ambrogio di Valpolicella
places.note: The western edge of the Classico zone towards the Adige and Garda, the marble quarry country of Valpolicella.

places.name: Valpantena
places.note: The valley directly north of Verona, east of the Classico zone, with its own label mention; the Bertani house's home.

places.name: Valpolicella orientale
places.note: The eastern valleys of Illasi, Mezzane and Tramigna: cooler and later, with a modern reputation for dense Amarone.

places.name: Soave
places.note: The hills and plain around Soave and Monteforte d'Alpone, east of Verona. Garganega at least 70%, with Trebbiano di Soave and Chardonnay allowed for the rest. Classico is the hill core; Colli Scaligeri the other hills; the plain makes the volume.

places.name: Soave Classico
places.note: Volcanic basalt on the Monteforte side, limestone around Soave's castle; the age-worthy wines, from pergola-trained old vines.

places.name: Monteforte d'Alpone
places.note: The volcanic commune: Foscarino and Froscà among the UGA.

places.name: Prosecco
places.note: Prosecco DOC spans nine provinces across Veneto and Friuli; Treviso and Trieste may appear on the label as subzones. The hills north of Treviso hold the two DOCGs.

places.name: Conegliano Valdobbiadene
places.note: The senior DOCG between the two towns, listed by UNESCO in 2019 for its steep hogback hills, with 43 Rive and the Cartizze hill.

places.name: Cartizze
places.note: A single hill of 107 hectares above Valdobbiadene between San Pietro di Barbozza, Santo Stefano and Saccol; the most expensive Prosecco land, traditionally made Dry.

places.name: Rive
places.note: The 43 named hamlets or communes; each bottle vintage dated and hand harvested.

places.name: Asolo
places.note: The smaller Prosecco DOCG west of the Piave around the hill town of Asolo, with its own Superiore.

places.name: Treviso
places.note: A subzone of Prosecco DOC; the plain's name on a label.

places.name: Bardolino
places.note: Garda's eastern shore on moraine: light Corvina reds, Bardolino Superiore DOCG and the pale Chiaretto di Bardolino rosé.

places.name: Custoza
places.note: South of Garda, a white blend of Garganega, Trebbiano, Tai and Cortese among others, on glacial moraine.

places.name: Lugana
places.note: The Garda south shore shared with Lombardy, where most of the zone lies; Turbiana on white clay.

places.name: Gambellara
places.note: The Garganega hills next door to Soave in the province of Vicenza, with Recioto di Gambellara DOCG.

places.name: Lessini Durello
places.note: Volcanic hills between Verona and Vicenza; Durella makes traditional method sparkling of fierce acidity.

places.name: Colli Euganei
places.note: Volcanic cones south of Padua: Bordeaux reds, Moscato Giallo as Fior d'Arancio DOCG, and Serprino, the local frizzante Glera.

places.name: Breganze
places.note: North of Vicenza: Vespaiolo, whose dried grapes make the sweet Torcolato.

places.name: Piave
places.note: The plain along the Piave east of Treviso: Raboso's Piave Malanotte DOCG and much Merlot.

places.name: Lison
places.note: Tai, which is Friulano, as a DOCG on the plain straddling Veneto and Friuli.

producers.name: Giuseppe Quintarelli
producers.why: Negrar's legend of Amarone and Recioto: long drying, long cask ageing, hand-written labels; the benchmark of traditional Valpolicella.

producers.name: Allegrini
producers.why: Fumane house that led the modern, Guyot-trained, single-vineyard Valpolicella: La Grola and the all-Corvina La Poja.

producers.name: Masi
producers.why: Gargagnago house whose Campofiorin (1964) brought the Ripasso technique to market and whose Costasera carried Amarone abroad.

producers.name: Bertani
producers.why: Founded 1857 in the Valpantena, among the first to sell Amarone from the late 1950s, with a famous library of old vintages.

producers.name: Tedeschi
producers.why: Pedemonte house known for the single-vineyard Monte Olmi Amarone.

producers.name: Bolla
producers.why: The Verona house, founded 1883, that put Soave and Valpolicella on American tables.

producers.name: Pieropan
producers.why: The Soave Classico house that proved Garganega ages: Calvarino and La Rocca since the 1970s.

producers.name: Inama
producers.why: Soave Classico from the volcanic Foscarino hill, plus Carmenère on the Colli Berici.

producers.name: Anselmi
producers.why: The Monteforte house that left the Soave DOC in 2000 to sell its Garganega as IGT in protest at the zone's rules.

producers.name: Gini
producers.why: Monteforte grower on old pergola vines; Contrada Salvarenza.

producers.name: Suavia
producers.why: Soave Classico from the high volcanic sites of Fittà.

producers.name: Bisol
producers.why: Valdobbiadene grower house with a long holding on Cartizze; Cartizze and the Rive bottlings.

producers.name: Nino Franco
producers.why: Valdobbiadene house founded 1919 that led the dry, vintage Prosecco movement: Rustico and the single-site Grave di Stecca.

producers.name: Carpenè Malvolti
producers.why: Conegliano house founded 1868 that first made Prosecco sparkling; its founder set up Italy's first school of oenology in Conegliano in 1876.

exam: Prosecco: Glera (85% minimum), tank method, DOC versus the two DOCGs, Cartizze, Rive, the sweetness scale and why Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut.
Valpolicella's blend and its four methods: Valpolicella, Ripasso, Amarone (dry), Recioto (sweet).
Amarone: appassimento, minimum alcohol, ageing, DOCG since 2010; Classico's five communes.
Soave: Garganega 70% minimum, Classico's volcanic hills, Soave Superiore and Recioto di Soave DOCG.
Bardolino and Chiaretto on Garda; Lugana shared with Lombardy.
Prosecco DOC Rosé (2020): Glera with 10 to 15% Pinot Nero, vintage dated.
Delle Venezie DOC (2017) as the Pinot Grigio umbrella for Veneto, Friuli and Trentino.
traps: Amarone is dry, Recioto is sweet; both come from the same dried grapes. The old chapter line is right.
Prosecco is a place and a method, Glera the grape since 2009; the village of Prosecco is in Friuli near Trieste, not in Veneto.
Extra Dry Prosecco is sweeter than Brut; Dry is sweeter still. Read the scale the other way from Champagne habits.
Ripasso is not made from dried grapes; it is normal Valpolicella passed over Amarone's spent skins.
Soave is a town and Garganega the grape; Soave Classico is a zone, Soave Superiore a separate DOCG, and the two do not mean the same thing.
Corvinone is its own variety, not a clone of Corvina; Molinara is no longer compulsory.
Valpolicella Superiore is a still wine with a year's age, not a Ripasso; Amarone Riserva takes four years.
Lugana belongs mostly to Lombardy; Bardolino and Custoza are the Veneto side of Garda.

cards.b: Corvina 45 to 95% (Corvinone may replace up to half of it), Rondinella 5 to 30%, balance from other local reds such as Molinara and Oseleta.

cards.f: Four wines, one blend, four methods
cards.b: Valpolicella: fresh. Ripasso: re-fermented on Amarone skins. Amarone: dried grapes fermented dry, 14% minimum (usually 15 plus). Recioto: dried grapes, fermentation stopped, sweet.

cards.b: DOCG 2010; appassimento; pressed no earlier than 1 December; 2 years' ageing (Riserva 4); Classico from Negrar, Fumane, Marano, Sant'Ambrogio, San Pietro in Cariano.
Prosecco DOC (9 provinces, Veneto and Friuli); Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore DOCG and Asolo Prosecco DOCG; Rive (43, vintage, hand picked); Superiore di Cartizze (one hill, 107 ha).
Glera, 85% minimum; Martinotti tank method; Brut Nature, Extra Brut, Brut (under 12 g/l), Extra Dry (12 to 17), Dry (17 to 32), Demi-Sec (32 to 50).

Garganega 70% minimum, Trebbiano di Soave and Chardonnay allowed. Soave DOC; Classico (Soave and Monteforte hills); Colli Scaligeri; Soave Superiore DOCG; Recioto di Soave DOCG (1998, Veneto's first).
Created 2020: Glera with 10 to 15% Pinot Nero, vintage dated, at least 60 days' second fermentation in tank, Brut Nature to Extra Dry only.
Bardolino (Corvina-led light red, Bardolino Superiore DOCG), Chiaretto di Bardolino rosé, Custoza white blend; Lugana is mostly Lombardy.
A sweet wine from dried grapes; from recia, Veronese dialect for ear, the ripest outer wings of the bunch once chosen for drying.

questions.q: Which grape leads the Valpolicella blend?
questions.exp: Corvina is 45 to 95% of Valpolicella, Rondinella 5 to 30%; Molinara is now optional and Oseleta a minor addition for colour and tannin.

questions.q: Which wine is Valpolicella re-fermented on the skins left from Amarone?
questions.exp: Ripasso passes finished Valpolicella over Amarone or Recioto pomace. Superiore is a year-aged still wine, Recioto the sweet dried-grape wine, Classico the historic zone.

questions.q: Which Prosecco sweetness level holds 12 to 17 grams of sugar per litre?
questions.exp: Extra Dry is 12 to 17 g/l, sweeter than Brut (under 12) and Brut Nature (under 3); Dry runs 17 to 32 and Demi-Sec 32 to 50. The scale reads the opposite way from what the words suggest.

questions.q: Name the grape of Soave.
questions.exp: Soave is at least 70% Garganega, with Trebbiano di Soave and Chardonnay permitted for the balance; Classico comes from the volcanic and limestone hills of Soave and Monteforte.

questions.q: What is the name of the single hill at the top of the Prosecco pyramid in Valdobbiadene?
questions.exp: Superiore di Cartizze is one hill of 107 hectares between San Pietro di Barbozza, Santo Stefano and Saccol, the most prized site of Conegliano Valdobbiadene.

questions.q: What is the minimum share of Glera in a wine labelled Prosecco?
questions.exp: Prosecco must be at least 85% Glera; the balance may come from Verdiso, Bianchetta, Perera, Glera Lunga, Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Grigio or Pinot Nero. Soave sets a 70% floor for Garganega, a figure often confused with it.

questions.q: Which Valpolicella wine is sweet, made from dried grapes with the fermentation stopped?
questions.exp: Recioto is the sweet ancestor of Amarone: the same appassimento grapes, fermentation halted with sugar left. Amarone is the same must taken to dryness.

questions.q: Which lake moderates the Bardolino and Custoza vineyards?
questions.exp: Bardolino lies on Garda's eastern shore and Custoza on the moraine just south of it. Iseo warms Franciacorta and Como lies below Valtellina, both in Lombardy.

regions.name: Friuli
regions.summary: Friuli Venezia Giulia is the far north-eastern corner: Alps behind, Adriatic in front, Slovenia along the hills. It is Italy's white wine conscience, varietal, precise, dry whites from Friulano, Ribolla Gialla, Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon, Pinot Bianco and Malvasia Istriana, made in the cold-fermented, reductive style the region pioneered in Italy in the 1960s. The two hill DOCs, Collio and Friuli Colli Orientali, on the marl and sandstone called ponca, carry the reputation; the gravel plain of Grave and Isonzo carries the volume. The same hills started the modern orange wine movement, and the Colli Orientali keep Friuli's reds, Schioppettino, Refosco and Pignolo, and its sweet Picolit and Ramandolo.

terroir.climate: Cool to moderate and wet: the Alps shelter the region from the north but the Adriatic sends humidity and rain, and Friuli is among Italy's rainiest wine regions. The hills see large day-night swings that keep aroma and acid; the Carso plateau above Trieste is scoured by the Bora, a cold, dry north-easterly. Hail and harvest rain are the hazards.
terroir.soils: Ponca, the local name for flysch, alternating layers of marl and sandstone laid down under an Eocene sea, defines Collio and the Colli Orientali: it crumbles, drains and holds water at depth. The Grave and Isonzo plains are deep alluvial gravel dropped by the Tagliamento, Meduna and Isonzo rivers, warm by day and quick to drain. Carso is red, iron-rich clay in pockets of limestone karst.
terroir.topography: A crescent of low hills from Cividale through Cormòns to Gorizia along the Slovenian border, rarely above 300 metres, where the best whites grow; a broad flat plain south and west of them to the sea; the Carso limestone plateau above Trieste; and the pre-Alps behind, where Ramandolo sits on the foothills near Nimis.
terroir.water: The Tagliamento and Isonzo rivers built the gravel plains and name the Grave and Isonzo zones; the lagoons of Grado and Marano and the Gulf of Trieste bring sea air to the south. The Bora off the karst keeps the Carso dry.

grapes.name: Friulano
grapes.styles: The native white, Sauvignonasse by DNA and Tocai Friulano until the name was lost in 2007: pear, almond, a bitter-nut finish, medium acid; the region's own glass with prosciutto di San Daniele.

grapes.name: Ribolla Gialla
grapes.styles: A high-acid, lemon-and-flower white of Collio and Oslavia, grown as Rebula across the border; the grape of the orange wine movement and of Friuli's sparkling boom.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Friuli's commercial engine, better than the plain average when from Collio or Isonzo: pear, nectarine, weight; also made as a coppery ramato with brief skin contact.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Grassy, flinty and ripe from the hills; the Collio's most sought-after international white.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Pinot Bianco: creamy and discreet, the quiet partner in Collio Bianco blends and a fine varietal in Isonzo.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Widely planted, often part of the great white blends.

grapes.name: Malvasia Istriana
grapes.styles: An aromatic, salty Malvasia of Carso and Collio, apricot and herbs.

grapes.name: Verduzzo
grapes.styles: A tannic white making dry wine and the sweet Ramandolo on the foothills.

grapes.name: Picolit
grapes.styles: A sweet white of tiny yields, the eighteenth-century dessert wine of European courts; Colli Orientali del Friuli Picolit DOCG.

grapes.name: Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso
grapes.styles: The native red with the red stem: dark, plummy, high acid, a bitter edge; the everyday red of plain and hills.

grapes.name: Schioppettino
grapes.styles: Prepotto's peppery, violet-scented red, revived from a few vines in the 1970s; also called Ribolla Nera.

grapes.name: Pignolo
grapes.styles: A rare, intensely tannic red of Rosazzo revived for long ageing.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The most planted red of the region, soft and fruity on the plain.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Much of Friuli's Cabernet Franc proved to be Carmenère; leafy, red-fruited and light.

grapes.name: Vitovska
grapes.styles: Carso's white, lean and saline, often skin fermented.

grapes.name: Terrano
grapes.styles: Carso's red, a Refosco relative, sharp and iron-rich.

grapes.name: Glera
grapes.styles: The village of Prosecco sits above Trieste, which is why the Prosecco DOC takes in all of Friuli.

wines.note: Dry, medium weight, pear, white peach and a bitter almond close; the local aperitivo with prosciutto and frico.
The hills' blended white, Friulano, Ribolla, Pinot Bianco, Sauvignon and more, often the estate's top cuvée and sometimes oaked.

made.viticulture: Vines on the hills are Guyot trained on ponca terraces that crumble and need constant rebuilding; on the gravel plain rows are longer and often machine harvested. Whites are picked early for acid in a wet climate, and the growers' chief enemy is rot, so canopies are opened, bunches thinned and sprays timed to the rain. Picolit's flowers abort, so a bunch carries a handful of berries and the yield per vine is tiny, which is why the wine is rare and dear. Verduzzo for Ramandolo is picked late and partly dried. Schioppettino, Pignolo and Tazzelenghe were nearly lost after phylloxera and the wars and were replanted from relic vines from the 1970s. The Carso's vines grow in pockets of red earth among the limestone, braced against the Bora; Vitovska and Terrano are its own.
made.winemaking: The modern Friulian white took shape in the 1960s: cold, slow fermentation in stainless steel under protection from oxygen, clean yeast, little or no malolactic, early bottling, varietal purity on the label. That became the template for Italian white wine. The region then went two further ways. The hills' top blends (Collio Bianco and the famous estate cuvées) took barrel fermentation and lees ageing for texture. And Oslavia, a hamlet of Collio above Gorizia, turned back towards the oldest method: Ribolla Gialla and Pinot Grigio fermented on their skins for weeks or months, in open wood or in Georgian clay amphorae buried in the ground, no additions, no temperature control, long ageing, and bottled amber and tannic. That is orange wine, and these are the wines the name was coined for. Sweet wines are late harvest or partly dried (Picolit, Ramandolo, Verduzzo). Ribolla sparkling is tank method; Pinot Grigio ramato takes a few hours of skin contact for a copper tint.

law.classification: The hills carry two senior DOCs, Collio (or Collio Goriziano, 1968) in the province of Gorizia and Friuli Colli Orientali (1970) in the province of Udine, both named for their marl hills and both varietal-led: the grape name follows the zone name on the label. The plain is covered by Friuli Grave (the largest), Friuli Isonzo, Friuli Aquileia, Friuli Latisana and Friuli Annia, with Carso above Trieste and Lison-Pramaggiore shared with Veneto. Friuli DOC, created in 2016, blankets the whole region for varietal wines and sparkling Ribolla Gialla. Four DOCGs are all small: Ramandolo (2001, sweet Verduzzo), Colli Orientali del Friuli Picolit (2006), Rosazzo (2011, a Friulano-led white blend) and Lison (Tai, shared with Veneto). Delle Venezie DOC (2017) takes the plain's Pinot Grigio across three regions, and the Prosecco DOC reaches the whole region.

places.name: Collio
places.note: The arc of hills around Cormòns and Gorizia along the Slovenian border, continued as Brda on the other side. Ponca soils, Guyot training, and some of the finest Friulano, Ribolla Gialla, Sauvignon, Pinot Bianco and Pinot Grigio in Italy, plus the Collio Bianco blends; DOC since 1968.

places.name: Oslavia
places.note: The hamlet above Gorizia where Ribolla Gialla on the skins became orange wine from the late 1990s, with amphorae from Georgia; the Gravner and Radikon hill.

places.name: Cormòns
places.note: The market town at the centre of Collio; Capriva, Dolegna and San Floriano around it hold the great estates.

places.name: Friuli Colli Orientali
places.note: The hills of the province of Udine from Cividale north to Tarcento, on the same ponca, cooler and more varied, with the region's native reds and sweet wines. DOC since 1970 as Colli Orientali del Friuli, renamed in 2011.

places.name: Rosazzo
places.note: An abbey hill south of Cividale: Rosazzo DOCG (a Friulano-led white blend) and the Pignolo and Ribolla subzones.

places.name: Prepotto
places.note: Schioppettino's home valley on the border; Schioppettino di Prepotto is a named subzone.

places.name: Cialla
places.note: A side valley with its own subzone for Picolit, Verduzzo and Schioppettino; a single estate revived it from 1970.

places.name: Ramandolo
places.note: On the foothills above Nimis and Tarcento: sweet Verduzzo, DOCG since 2001, Friuli's first.

places.name: Buttrio
places.note: A commune south of Udine with small, high-priced estates on ponca.

places.name: Friuli Isonzo
places.note: The gravel terraces of the Isonzo river south of Gorizia, warmer than Collio and ripening fuller whites; Rive Alte and Rive di Giare are its subzones.

places.name: Friuli Grave
places.note: The gravel plain on both sides of the Tagliamento, reaching west to the Livenza, the largest share of the region's wine: Pinot Grigio, Merlot, Refosco, Friulano, clean and inexpensive.

places.name: Carso
places.note: The limestone karst plateau above Trieste, red earth in pockets of rock, the Bora wind: Vitovska and Malvasia whites, Terrano red, much of it skin fermented; the village of Prosecco lies on its edge.

places.name: The lagoon plain
places.note: Friuli Aquileia, Friuli Latisana and Friuli Annia, the DOCs of the flat land towards the lagoons: light reds and whites for early drinking.

places.name: Lison-Pramaggiore
places.note: The plain shared with Veneto along the Livenza: Lison DOCG for Tai, and Merlot and Refosco under DOC.
